doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Weaned off changes; Pharoah Sanders at Café Wha? and Sun Ra's own labels
summary: Sun Ra preferred players without a bebop foundation; Harrison recalls Pharoah's early days, then admires Sun Ra's recording and independent labels.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: My spirituality. You know, so he had to wean me off of that foundation. And then I noticed a lot of guys, he was using a lot of musicians but he liked the guys that didn’t have that foundation so much. You know he gravitated to those guys because it was less work to re-indoctrinate you know. Same with John Coltrane. John Coltrane liked Pharoah because he hadn’t had the bebop foundation so much. Pharoah was like a blues kind of guy from Arkansas. And he was — me and Pharoah, he was a year older than me. He was a year older than I. He was born in ’41, I was born in 1942. And we had gotten to, came to New York on the same day. He was coming from San Francisco, Oakland, California and I was coming from Detroit. And I think the first gig we had I think Pharoah was working with Sun Ra and he started working with Sun Ra before I did, and he was working at Café Wha? There’s a club called Café Wha? in the Village, and when he wasn’t working with Sun Ra he was washing dishes in the place. You know. And you know we were kids trying to find our way. And one time he was asking for his own showcase, his own performance. And the owner gave him a night, I think it was maybe a Monday night or something like that. And Pharoah for his rhythm section he chose the Blue Note all star group: Billy Higgins, and so I said what? And I didn’t think much of it at that time but thinking about Pharoah, his perception of himself, he always had a big image of himself and how he wanted to present himself you know. And that’s very important, he had that concept of himself that I think is very important in terms of being a leader. And you know they had to pay these guys and it was more than they expected to pay. Pharoah said, “You’ve got to pay my band.” You know. And then at that point he was working with Sun Ra and then around different groups and then John Coltrane, he

was hanging out with John Coltrane. John liked him you know. So he did more and more with John and John started using him on gigs and whatnot, and he started touring and whatnot, the rest is history. Now with Sun Ra I used to make fun of Sun Ra but something that I really took serious when I saw he was recording everything you know. Rehearsals. And he had two record labels. You know he was producing and marketing his music, and his music was in the marketplace. Of course it was like a small niche fan base. But it was a fan base nevertheless that he nurtured. I guess he got started in Chicago. He was nurturing this fan base and he didn’t care anything about conforming to the status quo at that time, of the major record companies in terms of being a contracted artist for a major label. He didn’t want to do that because he would have to conform and play like a contemporary sound or a homogenized sound, that’s the way he would put it.
